title: Vase

altText: A small art-glass vase by Emile Gallé with a bird as part of its decoration. The glass has a smooth, polished look.

source.verifiedBy: Met Collection API object record: title, maker, date, medium, classification (Glass), tags (Birds), height, credit line, public-domain flag, and image URLs read from the record

context: A glass vase by Emile Gallé, the French designer from Nancy who became a leading figure of Art Nouveau glassmaking. The Met dates it to about 1890–1900 and tags it Birds. The vase is about 18.7 cm (7 3/8 inches) tall.

descriptions.k: This is a small glass vase. A bird is part of its picture. It was made in France a long time ago by an artist named Gallé. Can you find the bird? What do you think it is doing?
descriptions.g12: Emile Gallé made this glass vase in France about one hundred and thirty years ago. A bird is part of the design. Glass can be smooth, shiny, and full of color. Look for the bird and for the shape of the vase. What would you put in it?
descriptions.g35: Emile Gallé was a French artist who turned glass into art. He lived in the city of Nancy and loved plants, flowers, and animals. This vase, made around 1890 to 1900, has a bird in its design. Look for the bird and for the curves of the vase. How did the artist use glass instead of paint to make a picture?
descriptions.g68: Emile Gallé, working in Nancy, France, helped define the Art Nouveau style, which found beauty in plants, animals, and flowing curves. This vase of about 1890–1900 features a bird in its decoration, a subject Gallé's studio used often. Rather than painting a picture on a surface, a glassmaker builds color and detail into the material. How might a bird seem different when it is made of glass? What feelings does the vase give?
descriptions.g910: Gallé's vase of about 1890–1900 represents Art Nouveau's drive to bring nature into everyday design. The bird motif, noted in the Met record, connects the object to the movement's interest in animals and plants as sources of line, color, and mood. Because decoration is created in glass itself, the vase works as sculpture, picture, and container at once. Consider how scale, surface, and subject make an object that feels intimate, delicate, and carefully crafted.
descriptions.g1112: Emile Gallé's glass belongs to a late-nineteenth-century effort to treat decorative objects as serious art. This vase of about 1890–1900, tagged with a bird motif, reflects Art Nouveau's fascination with nature, but it also reflects the commercial ambitions of a studio producing work for collectors. The material both reveals and hides: light passes through it, yet colors and images are fixed inside. Ask how such works negotiate between individual artistry, studio production, and the market for luxury.

g1112.space: How does a decorated three-dimensional vessel complicate the idea of a single viewpoint?

teacherNote.context: Emile Gallé (1846–1904) of Nancy, France, was a leader of Art Nouveau glass and furniture. The Met record dates this vase to about 1890–1900 and tags it Birds.
directions: Have students sketch a vase that includes an animal and explain how the animal follows the vase's shape.
Ask students to compare painting on a surface with building color into a material like glass.
Discuss how a studio might share work among many hands while using one famous name.
